session.question: How does the study use predictive analytics in the 1-hop work, and what does the 2-hop AI impact assessment say about AI"s role for sustainable development?
session.answer:
In the 1-hop study, predictive analytics is used to build a classification model that forecasts which infected DBA/2 mice will develop malaria-associated acute lung injury/acute respiratory distress syndrome (ALI/ARDS) before death. The model relies on two measurable predictors: respiratory variables, specifically enhanced pause and respiratory frequency, and parasitemia. Using these inputs, the authors could retrospectively identify mice likely to die from ALI/ARDS as early as 7 days post-infection and distinguish ALI/ARDS from hyperparasitemia, with validation from associated biological findings such as higher VEGF levels and increased lung permeability. (ortolan2014predictivecriteriato chunk 1)

The 2-hop AI impact assessment concludes that AI has an overall positive effect on sustainable development. The Delphi study reports a consensus mean score of 78.8%, with highly positive impacts on SDGs 6, 7, 8, 9, 11, 13, 14, and 15; positive impacts on SDGs 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 10, and 12; and neutral effects on SDGs 16 and 17. The study therefore characterizes AI as a powerful enabler of sustainable development, particularly across health, education, infrastructure, and environmental domains. (ametepey2024theimpactof chunk 1)

session.context:
pqac-23354307: The excerpt explains that AI, especially machine learning and natural language processing, can significantly improve sustainable accounting by enhancing environmental impact assessment and reporting. It says AI enables automated processing of large, heterogeneous data sources such as IoT sensors, satellite imagery, and corporate disclosures, improving data accuracy, real-time monitoring, predictive analytics, and transparency in sustainability reporting. The paper frames AI as transformative for sustainable development because it helps organizations make informed decisions, comply with environmental regulations, reduce ecological footprints, and achieve sustainability goals. It also notes challenges like privacy, transparency, and cost, and stresses interdisciplinary collaboration.
From Beatrice Oyinkansola Adelakun, Bernard Owusu Antwi, Afari Ntiakoh, and Augustine Obinna Eziefule. Leveraging ai for sustainable accounting: developing models for environmental impact assessment and reporting. Finance & Accounting Research Journal, 2024. URL: https://doi.org/10.51594/farj.v6i6.1234, doi:10.51594/farj.v6i6.1234.

pqac-d13f5bc7: The excerpt reports a Delphi study on AI’s impact on SDG implementation. Experts reached a consensus that AI has an overall positive impact on sustainable development, with a mean score of 78.8%. The assessment found highly positive impacts for SDGs 6, 7, 8, 9, 11, 13, 14, and 15; positive impacts for SDGs 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 10, and 12; and neutral scores for SDGs 16 and 17, suggesting more cautious consideration is needed there. The paper frames AI as a powerful tool for advancing sustainability goals across health, education, infrastructure, and environmental domains.
From Simon Ofori Ametepey, Clinton Aigbavboa, Wellington Didibhuku Thwala, and Hutton Addy. The impact of ai in sustainable development goal implementation: a delphi study. Sustainability, 2024. URL: https://doi.org/10.3390/su16093858, doi:10.3390/su16093858.

pqac-1c95d1b9: The study applies predictive analytics by building a model to forecast which infected DBA/2 mice will develop malaria-associated ALI/ARDS before death. It uses two measurable criteria—breathing patterns (enhanced pause and respiratory frequency) and parasitemia—as predictive variables. Based on these predictors, the researchers could retrospectively classify sacrificed mice as likely to die from ALI/ARDS as early as 7 days post-infection. The method helped distinguish ALI/ARDS from hyperparasitemia and was validated with associated findings such as higher VEGF levels and increased lung permeability in predicted ALI/ARDS cases.
From Luana S. Ortolan, Michelle K. Sercundes, Renato Barboza, Daniela Debone, Oscar Murillo, Stefano C. F. Hagen, Momtchilo Russo, Maria Regina D' Império Lima, José M. Alvarez, Marcos Amaku, Claudio R. F. Marinho, and Sabrina Epiphanio. Predictive criteria to study the pathogenesis of malaria-associated ali/ards in mice. Mediators of Inflammation, 2014. URL: https://doi.org/10.1155/2014/872464, doi:10.1155/2014/872464.

pqac-5b7d839f: The excerpt says that AI generally promotes sustainable development during urbanization across 51 countries. The strongest positive effect comes from AI R&D innovation, followed by AI infrastructure, while AI market advantage has the smallest positive impact overall. The study also finds heterogeneity: AI’s promotion is strongest in upper-middle sustainable development countries (60%–70% quantiles). Urbanization changes the effect: below the urbanization threshold, AI infrastructure and R&D innovation support sustainable development while market advantage inhibits it; above the threshold, infrastructure inhibits it, R&D innovation becomes insignificant, and market advantage turns positive.
From Qiang Wang, Fuyu Zhang, and Rongrong Li. Artificial intelligence and sustainable development during urbanization: perspectives on ai r&d innovation, ai infrastructure, and ai market advantage. Sustainable Development, 2024. URL: https://doi.org/10.1002/sd.3150, doi:10.1002/sd.3150.

pqac-47974752: The paper’s predictive analytics approach is used to analyze and classify student behavior in e-learning so instructors can track attention levels and identify learners who may be failing or uninterested. The system detects students using Viola–Jones, isolates occlusions with a region-shrinking technique, verifies objects via template matching, extracts skeleton and silhouette features, and then uses a genetic algorithm to categorize behavior. The goal is to support targeted interventions and improve learning outcomes. It reports average accuracies of 90.5% on MED and 85.7% on Edu-Net datasets.
From Naif Al Mudawi, Mahwish Pervaiz, Bayan Alabduallah, Abdulwahab Alazeb, Abdullah Alshahrani, Saud S. Alotaibi, and Ahmad Jalal. Predictive analytics for sustainable e-learning: tracking student behaviors. Sustainability, 2023. URL: https://doi.org/10.3390/su152014780, doi:10.3390/su152014780.

contexts.context: The excerpt describes a 2024 study on AI-induced job impact using data from 3,682 full-time workers. It examines perceptions of AI-related job displacement risk and AI’s complementary effects on labor, using an extended ordered probit model to identify which worker characteristics and industries are most affected. The findings suggest higher perceived risk among women, older, and more educated workers, as well as frequent internet users and remote workers. It also finds a potential complementary effect, where AI supports human labor rather than replacing it. However, the excerpt does not mention predictive analytics or any “1-hop work” methodology specifically.

contexts.context: The excerpt reports a Delphi study on AI’s impact on SDG implementation. Experts reached a consensus that AI has an overall positive impact on sustainable development, with a mean score of 78.8%. The assessment found highly positive impacts for SDGs 6, 7, 8, 9, 11, 13, 14, and 15; positive impacts for SDGs 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 10, and 12; and neutral scores for SDGs 16 and 17, suggesting more cautious consideration is needed there. The paper frames AI as a powerful tool for advancing sustainability goals across health, education, infrastructure, and environmental domains.

contexts.context: The excerpt describes AI-based decision aids as having both benefits and risks for sustainable development. It says personalized AI content can help consumers and businesses by making content more relevant, but it can also enable hidden interference and manipulation, reducing consumer autonomy. The paper frames consumer autonomy as a resource at risk and argues that sustainable AI should protect it through transparency, complementarity, and privacy regulation. Overall, it presents a constructive view: AI can support sustainable development only if its influence is balanced and ethical, especially in online decision-making.

session.formatted_answer:
Question: How does the study use predictive analytics in the 1-hop work, and what does the 2-hop AI impact assessment say about AI"s role for sustainable development?

In the 1-hop study, predictive analytics is used to build a classification model that forecasts which infected DBA/2 mice will develop malaria-associated acute lung injury/acute respiratory distress syndrome (ALI/ARDS) before death. The model relies on two measurable predictors: respiratory variables, specifically enhanced pause and respiratory frequency, and parasitemia. Using these inputs, the authors could retrospectively identify mice likely to die from ALI/ARDS as early as 7 days post-infection and distinguish ALI/ARDS from hyperparasitemia, with validation from associated biological findings such as higher VEGF levels and increased lung permeability. (ortolan2014predictivecriteriato chunk 1)

The 2-hop AI impact assessment concludes that AI has an overall positive effect on sustainable development. The Delphi study reports a consensus mean score of 78.8%, with highly positive impacts on SDGs 6, 7, 8, 9, 11, 13, 14, and 15; positive impacts on SDGs 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 10, and 12; and neutral effects on SDGs 16 and 17. The study therefore characterizes AI as a powerful enabler of sustainable development, particularly across health, education, infrastructure, and environmental domains. (ametepey2024theimpactof chunk 1)
